title: Matrices and Matrix Operations
objectives: Multiply a matrix by a vector and interpret the result as a linear combination of columns
Compute matrix-matrix products correctly and explain why multiplication does not commute
State and use the dimension rule for matrix products, and compute transposes including (AB)^T
Recognise identity, diagonal and symmetric matrices and their roles in financial models
motivation: A fund holds 500 assets; a market shock changes all 500 prices at once. Rewriting each price update separately is hopeless, so models package the whole update into one object: a matrix. Apply it to the vector of current prices and every asset updates in one operation. Matrices are also how regression, covariance and transition models are stored, so reading matrix notation, and multiplying matrices fluently, is a prerequisite for everything from Gaussian elimination to PCA.

blocks.text: A matrix is a machine that acts on vectors

blocks.md: A **matrix** is a rectangular array of numbers with $m$ rows and $n$ columns; we say it has shape $m \times n$. The deepest way to read it is as a **function from vectors to vectors**: an $m \times n$ matrix eats an $n$-vector and produces an $m$-vector. The output is defined by the **matrix-vector product**: entry $i$ of the result is the dot product of row $i$ with the input vector. Equivalently, and this is the reading worth internalising, the output is a **linear combination of the matrix's columns**, with the input's components as the weights.

blocks.tex: A x = \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} \\ a_{21} & a_{22} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{pmatrix} = x_1 \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} \\ a_{21} \end{pmatrix} + x_2 \begin{pmatrix} a_{12} \\ a_{22} \end{pmatrix}
blocks.caption: The two readings of Ax: row-by-row dot products, or a weighted mix of columns.

blocks.title: Worked example: a matrix acting on a vector
items: Row reading: first entry $= 2 \times 1 + 0 \times 2 = 2$; second entry $= 1 \times 1 + 3 \times 2 = 7$.
Both readings agree: $Ax = (2, 7)$. The matrix moved the vector; nothing was added that did not come from $A$ and $x$.

blocks.caption: This matrix shears the plane: vertical lines stay put while horizontal levels slide right. Drag a point and watch how Ax transforms it.

blocks.md: If $A$ and $B$ are both maps on vectors, applying $B$ first and then $A$ is itself a map, and it deserves a matrix. That matrix is the **product** $AB$, whose entry $(i, j)$ is the dot product of row $i$ of $A$ with column $j$ of $B$. The defining property to remember is the functional one: $(AB)x = A(Bx)$ - the product means "do $B$, then do $A$". The **dimension rule** follows: an $m \times n$ matrix can only accept $n$-vectors, so $(m \times n)(n \times p) = m \times p$; the inner dimensions must match and cancel.

blocks.title: Worked example: AB and BA, and why they differ
items: $AB \neq BA$: applying transformations in a different order gives a different transformation. Matrix multiplication is **not commutative**.

blocks.md: Addition and scalar multiplication of matrices are componentwise, exactly as for vectors, so $A + B = B + A$ *is* true, it is only multiplication that has an order. Powers of a matrix therefore mean repeated application: if $T$ is a one-step transition matrix for a market regime (bull/bear probabilities), then $T^2$ is the two-step matrix, because $T(Ts)$ applies one step, then another. This is how multi-period risk and Markov-chain models are built.

The **transpose** $A^\top$ flips a matrix over its diagonal: row $i$ becomes column $i$. It converts row-vector conventions into column-vector ones and appears in every variance formula. Transposing a product **reverses the order**: $(AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top$ - think of it as undoing "do $B$ then $A$", which you undo by doing $A^\top$ then $B^\top$. The **identity matrix** $I$ has ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere, and acts as the number 1: $AI = IA = A$. A **diagonal** matrix scales each coordinate independently, and a **symmetric** matrix satisfies $A = A^\top$ - the shape every covariance matrix has, since $\text{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = \text{Cov}(X_j, X_i)$.

rows: Pairwise asset risk; diagonal entries are variances
$n \times n$, rows or columns sum to 1
n assets, k factors; inner dimension = number of factors

blocks.title: The transpose of a product reverses order
blocks.md: $(AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top$, never $A^\top B^\top$. The same reversal shows up later in the inverse formula $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$. If your algebra keeps this "socks-then-shoes, shoes-then-socks" rule in mind, half the classic sign/order errors in derivations disappear.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2, 0], [1, 3]])
B = np.array([[1, 4], [2, 5]])
print((A @ B).tolist())      # [[2, 8], [7, 19]]
print((B @ A).tolist())      # [[6, 12], [9, 15]] - order matters
print((A @ B).T.tolist())    # [[2, 7], [8, 19]] - transpose of the product
blocks.caption: The @ operator multiplies matrices; .T transposes. Compare with the by-hand results above.

guidedExercise.prompt: Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Compute $AB$, then compute $B^\top A^\top$ and confirm that it equals $(AB)^\top$.
hints: Entry (i, j) of AB is row i of A dotted with column j of B.
Transpose each factor first, then multiply in the reversed order.
guidedExercise.solution: $AB$: (1,1): $(1,2)\cdot(2,1) = 4$; (1,2): $(1,2)\cdot(0,1) = 2$; (2,1): $(0,3)\cdot(2,1) = 3$; (2,2): $(0,3)\cdot(0,1) = 3$. So $AB = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 3 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $(AB)^\top = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$. Now $B^\top A^\top = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$: (1,1) $= 2 + 2 = 4$; (1,2) $= 0 + 3 = 3$; (2,1) $= 0 + 2 = 2$; (2,2) $= 0 + 3 = 3$. This gives $\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ - matching $(AB)^\top$ exactly.

independentExercise.prompt: Market regimes are Bull (B) and Bear (R). The column-stochastic transition matrix $M = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.4 \\ 0.2 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$ sends a state vector to next month's state (columns sum to 1). Today's state is $s = (0.7, 0.3)$ (probability of Bull, Bear). Compute next month's state $Ms$, and the state after two months $M^2 s$ (compute $M^2$ first).
hints: $Ms$: entry 1 uses column 1 of M, entry 2 uses column 2.
M^2 means M times M, four dot products, then apply M again to the result.

commonMistakes: Multiplying matrices in the wrong order - $AB$ and $BA$ are different transformations.
Multiplying shapes that do not match: an $m \times n$ matrix cannot act on an $m$-vector, only on an $n$-vector.
Writing $(AB)^\top = A^\top B^\top$ instead of $B^\top A^\top$.
Reading $A^2$ as squaring each entry instead of multiplying the matrix by itself.
realWorldApplication: Graphics engines, risk engines and regression libraries all reduce to matrix products; a GPU's headline strength is multiplying large matrices very fast, because that is what most models actually compute.
quantFinanceApplication: A covariance matrix, a factor-exposure matrix and a multi-step transition matrix are three views of the same object class: $n \times n$ or $n \times k$ arrays acting on position vectors. Portfolio variance $w^\top C w$ is a vector-matrix-vector sandwich built entirely from the operations in this lesson.
summary: An $m \times n$ matrix is a map from $n$-vectors to $m$-vectors; $Ax$ is both a stack of row dot products and a linear combination of columns.
Matrix multiplication is composition: $(AB)x = A(Bx)$, so $(m \times n)(n \times p) = m \times p$, and in general $AB \neq BA$.
Transposes reverse product order: $(AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top$; the identity $I$ is the neutral element of multiplication.
Symmetric matrices ($A = A^\top$) are the natural shape for covariance and similarity structures; powers $T^k$ model repeated transitions.

quiz.prompt: A $3 \times 2$ matrix multiplies a $2 \times 5$ matrix. What is the shape of the product?
quiz.explanation: Inner dimensions (2 and 2) match and cancel, leaving the outer dimensions: $3 \times 5$.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about square matrices $A$ and $B$ is ALWAYS true?
quiz.explanation: Addition is componentwise, so transposing a sum just transposes each term. The transpose of a product reverses order ($(AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top$), and $AB = BA$ can fail, as the worked example showed.

quiz.prompt: For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $x = (2, 5)$, what is the first entry of $Ax$?
quiz.explanation: Row 1 of A dotted with x: $3 \times 2 + 1 \times 5 = 11$. (The second entry is $0 + 2 \times 5 = 10$.)

quiz.prompt: Select every statement that is true for all square matrices (where the operation is defined):
quiz.explanation: Multiplication by the identity is neutral, transposes reverse order, and addition is associative (it is componentwise). $AB = BA$ is the odd one out: order matters for multiplication.

quiz.prompt: What does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2, 0], [1, 3]])
B = np.array([[1, 4], [2, 5]])
print((A @ B).tolist())
print((A @ np.array([1, 2])).tolist())

quiz.prompt: Give one concrete reason (an example or an interpretation) why $AB \neq BA$ in general.
quiz.modelAnswer: AB means "apply B first, then A"; reversing the order of two transformations generally gives a different transformation, e.g. a shear followed by a rotation is not the same as the rotation followed by the shear.
quiz.explanation: Products are compositions, and composing maps in different orders gives different maps, exactly as the worked example showed numerically ($AB = [[2,8],[7,19]]$ but $BA = [[6,12],[9,15]]$).

flashcards.front: Two ways to read the matrix-vector product Ax
flashcards.back: Rows: entry i is row i of A dotted with x. Columns: Ax is a linear combination of A's columns with weights from x.
$(AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top$ - the order reverses (socks-then-shoes rule).
$(m \times n)(n \times p) = m \times p$; the inner dimensions must match and are 'consumed'.
Because it is composition of transformations: doing B then A differs from doing A then B.
[[2, 8], [7, 19]], row of A dotted with column of B, entry by entry.
